title: Closed Thursday, Back Monday: Thanksgiving Week Layovers, TONUs and the Accessorials U.S. Fleets Can Actually Collect in 2026
summary: Closed docks, pushed appointments and canceled tenders make Thanksgiving week an accessorial fight. How U.S. carriers and brokers protect layover and TONU pay.
body_markdown:
The text comes in at 9:40 p.m. on the Monday before Thanksgiving.


"Receiver pushed your Wednesday 0600. New appt Friday 1400. Sorry."


You run operations for a 60-truck van and reefer fleet out of central Ohio. The truck in question is a reefer loaded with dairy, already 400 miles into a run to a grocery DC outside Philadelphia. The driver was supposed to deliver Wednesday morning, reload Wednesday afternoon, and be home for dinner Thursday.


Now he's going to spend Thanksgiving in a truck stop lot with the reefer running.


You're made up for this story. The text isn't. Some version of it lands on dispatch boards all over the United States this week, and what you do in the next 12 hours decides whether that holiday costs you a few hundred dollars of unrecovered time or a driver, a customer and a month of billing disputes.


## Monday night: the push you could have seen coming


Here's the uncomfortable part. That push wasn't really a surprise.


The national auto club's Thanksgiving forecast, released Nov. 16, 2026, expects 81.5 million Americans to travel at least 50 miles between Tuesday, Nov. 24 and Monday, Nov. 30. About 72.9 million of them will drive.


What that means for you: the receiver's own staff is part of that number. DCs run thin crews on Wednesday, close or skeleton-staff on Thursday, and spend Friday digging out. Traffic-data analysts quoted in the same forecast expect Tuesday and Wednesday afternoons to be the worst on the road, with metros like New York and Boston seeing more than double normal congestion.


So your driver is fighting the I-76 and I-95 crawl at exactly the moment the dock is shrinking its schedule. Appointments get consolidated. Late-booked loads get bumped. Yours was booked late.


Demand isn't letting up, either. The largest U.S. retail trade group forecast on Oct. 15 that November and December retail sales will grow 4.2% over 2025, to about $1.013 trillion. More product flowing into fewer staffed hours means more pushes, not fewer.


Which brings you to the first real decision of the night. What does this push cost, and who's going to pay for it?


## Tuesday, 6 a.m.: reading the rate con like a lawyer


You pull the rate confirmation. The load came through a broker, and the accessorial language is the usual two lines: "Detention $50/hr after 2 hours free. Layover $150/day after 24 hours, with prior approval."


Read that again, the way the broker's billing team will in January.


"After 24 hours." Measured from what? The original appointment? The driver's arrival? The receiver's new appointment? "With prior approval." Approved by whom, and in what form? A dispatcher's "ok" in a text thread? An email? A note in the broker's portal?


This is where most holiday layovers die. Not because anyone argues they weren't real, but because nobody can prove the trigger was met in the exact way the paper requires.


The money is not trivial. Published broker terms for layover pay to carriers typically land between $150 and $360 a day, and one large asset carrier's published tariff, effective Oct. 1, 2026, bills shippers $750 a day for a solo-driver layover. That spread tells you something. The same truck sitting in the same lot is worth $150 on one piece of paper and $750 on another.


What that means for you: the holiday layover is decided at the moment of the tender, not the moment of the push. If your standard terms don't spell out when the clock starts, what counts as approval, and whether a facility closure counts as a layover event, you're negotiating from memory against someone negotiating from a contract.


So at 6 a.m. you do the only thing that actually helps. You email the broker's after-hours desk, quote their own rate con language, state the original appointment, the new appointment, the driver's location and the reefer setpoint, and ask for written approval of layover for Wednesday through Friday.


Then you turn to the driver.


## Tuesday, mid-morning: the clock nobody bills


The driver's question is simpler than the broker's. "Do I sit, or do I come home?"


He can't do both. Sitting means three days burning reefer fuel at a truck stop while his family eats without him. Coming home means deadheading a loaded reefer somewhere secure, or dropping it, and paying for it.


Here's what the hours look like from the driver's side. Under federal hours-of-service rules, waiting at a facility or for an appointment is on-duty time if he's working or responsible for the load, and it still eats into the 14-hour window. A holiday layover can be logged as off duty when he's genuinely relieved, but the day still isn't driving, and he still isn't earning miles.


An industry research institute's 2024 detention study found that truckload drivers lost about 173 hours to detention in 2023 and roughly $889 in income even after detention pay. Its 2026 operating-cost update estimated that figure rose to $962 per driver in 2025, with carriers losing $5,392 per truck.


What that means for you: every unpaid day at a closed dock comes straight out of a paycheck your driver can see. Thanksgiving is the week they notice most, because it's the week they had a plan.


That same 2024 study found that while most carriers charge detention, facilities paid fewer than half of the invoices carriers submitted. Layover is worse, because it's rarer, messier and easier to deny.


So you make a call. You'll pay the driver a holiday layover rate out of your own pocket starting Wednesday, whether or not the broker approves, and you'll fight for recovery separately. Your driver settlement and your customer billing are two different decisions. Shops that tie them together end up asking drivers to absorb disputes they had no control over.


Then the second load blows up.


## Tuesday, noon: the TONU that arrives three hours late


A van was dispatched at 5 a.m. to a pickup in Indiana for a Wednesday delivery. At 8:15 a.m., with the truck 40 miles out, the shipper's coordinator calls the broker. Order canceled. Nothing to load.


The broker calls you at 11:50 a.m.


That's a truck ordered, not used. Published broker terms for TONU to carriers commonly sit between $150 and $250, with some shippers' carrier guides capping it at $150 when the cancellation comes with less than 12 hours' notice. The same large carrier's tariff bills shippers $350.


What that means for you: on a Thanksgiving Tuesday, $150 doesn't come close to covering what the truck lost. Diesel averaged $5.937 a gallon nationally in the week of Nov. 16, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. That's down three straight weeks but still $2.069 higher than a year earlier. Forty deadhead miles and a dead morning cost real money before you've even thought about the reload you can no longer get, because by noon on the Tuesday before Thanksgiving, the decent freight is gone.


The fight here is about timestamps. When was the truck dispatched? When did the shipper cancel? When did the broker tell you? If the shipper canceled at 8:15 a.m. and you heard at 11:50 a.m., those three and a half hours belong to someone, and it shouldn't be you.


Brokers have a version of this problem too. If you're on the brokerage side, you just learned your shipper owes you a TONU you may not have written into the shipper contract. You're about to pay a carrier for a cancellation you can't bill upstream.


That gap, between what you promised the carrier and what your customer promised you, is where holiday margin goes to die. And it's set months before November.


## Wednesday: why every shop answers these questions differently


By Wednesday afternoon, you have the broker's reply on the layover. Approved for Thursday and Friday. Not Wednesday, because the "24 hours" runs from the original 6 a.m. appointment.


You can live with that. What strikes you is how differently the same week plays out depending on who you are.


**If you run an asset fleet,** the holiday question is mostly about drivers and equipment. Do you pay layover regardless of recovery? Do you let a reefer sit three days on a truck stop lot, or move it to a secure yard? Do you pre-book Friday reloads near receivers you know will push?


**If you run a brokerage,** the holiday question is mostly about contracts. Do your shipper agreements pass through layover and TONU at the rates your carrier rate cons promise? Do your reps know which receivers close Thursday and which close Wednesday at noon? Who on your team can approve a layover at 9 p.m. on a Monday?


**If you run a hybrid,** you get both problems, plus a third: the temptation to move a stranded asset load to a broker carrier, or the reverse, without anyone checking what the accessorial terms say on either side.


None of these answers is universal. A grocery-heavy reefer carrier and a building-products flatbed fleet face completely different holiday weeks. A brokerage that lives on spot freight and one built around a few contract shippers have different exposure. Your customer mix, your driver pay model, your facility list and your contracts make your Thanksgiving week yours.


Which is exactly why a generic process breaks here. The rules that matter (which facilities close when, what triggers layover, who can approve it, how a TONU gets timestamped) are specific to your business. They only work if they live in your system as rules, not in a dispatcher's head.


## Friday, 2 p.m.: what the shops that collect do differently


The reefer delivers Friday at 2:40 p.m. Forty minutes past the appointment, because the dock is buried. The broker's January dispute will mention it.


Here's what you'd want in place before next year. Not a wish list. The specific things carriers and brokers who actually collect holiday accessorials tend to have.


**A holiday facility calendar that drives booking.** Every receiver's Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year's hours, captured in October, attached to the facility record and checked when a load books. If a Wednesday appointment lands at a receiver that's historically pushed, the load gets flagged before anyone tenders a truck to it.


**Accessorial terms that define the trigger, not just the rate.** When does layover start? From the original appointment or the arrival time? Does a facility closure count? What counts as approval? Write it into your standard terms and your rate cons so nobody has to interpret it in January.


**Timestamps captured as events, not reconstructed later.** Dispatch time, arrival time, push notification time, cancellation time, approval time. If those live in a text thread, you'll lose the argument. If they're captured as statuses on the load, the invoice builds itself.


**Approval permissions that match the calendar.** Somebody needs authority to approve or request a layover at 9:40 p.m. on a holiday Monday. Decide who, and give their approvals the same weight in the system as a daytime rep's.


**Driver settlement decoupled from customer recovery.** Pay drivers on your policy. Chase customers on theirs. Track the gap so you know which lanes and customers cost you money every holiday.


**Pass-through rules for brokers.** If a carrier rate con includes TONU or layover, the matching shipper contract should too, at a margin you chose. A rule that flags a mismatch at booking saves an argument at billing.


None of this is exotic. It's just specific. And specificity is what a stock workflow doesn't give you, because it was built for an average shop, not yours.


## The takeaway: the holiday is decided in October


By the following Monday, your reefer driver is home, and the layover invoice is sitting in the broker's queue with every timestamp attached. You'll probably collect two of the three days. You'll definitely collect the TONU, because you documented the cancellation timeline.


That's a decent result. It isn't a great one.


A great one happens when the push gets flagged before booking, the layover terms answer every question in advance, and the holiday costs you a known, priced amount instead of an argument. That comes from deciding, months before the text arrives, how your business handles closed docks, canceled tenders and approvals after hours, then making sure your system enforces those decisions instead of hoping people remember them.


Thanksgiving is one week. Christmas and New Year's are next. Every one of them rewards the shops that wrote down their own rules.


## Frequently asked questions


### What's the difference between detention and layover over Thanksgiving?


Detention pays by the hour for waiting past free time on the same day, while layover pays a flat daily amount when a truck can't load or unload until a later day. Over Thanksgiving week, a single load can generate both: hours of detention Wednesday, then layover when the receiver closes Thursday and reschedules to Friday.


### Is a holiday facility closure automatically a layover event?


No, it depends entirely on how your rate confirmation or contract defines the layover trigger. Many rate cons start layover only after 24 hours from the original appointment and require prior approval, so a closure may not qualify unless your terms say it does. Define closures explicitly in your standard terms.


### How much is a typical TONU in 2026?


Published broker terms commonly pay carriers $150 to $250 for a truck ordered, not used, while carrier tariffs billing shippers run higher, around $350 in at least one large carrier's published tariff. The rate con controls what's owed, so set the number and the notice window before dispatch.


### Do drivers have to log holiday layover time as on duty?


Not always. Under federal hours-of-service rules, time a driver is genuinely relieved of all duty and responsibility for the load can be logged as off duty, while waiting to load or unload is generally on duty and counts against the 14-hour window. How you log it affects both compliance and driver pay, so set a clear policy.


### How can brokers avoid paying TONUs they can't bill to shippers?


Match your shipper contracts to the accessorial terms in your carrier rate cons, and flag mismatches when the load books. If a carrier rate con promises a TONU or layover, your shipper agreement should pass that charge through at a margin you chose, not one you discover in January.
